title: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952)
shortTitle: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952)
summary: The President has no inherent power to seize private property to avert a strike; his power to act must come from a statute or from the Constitution, and here neither supplied it.
notes:
Key line: The President's power, if any, to issue the order must stem either from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself. (Justice Black)

Citation: 343 U.S. 579 (1952).

Cornell LII Wex on this case (https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/youngstown_sheet_tube_co._v._sawyer_(1952)): Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer 343 U.S. 579 (1952) was a case in which the U.S. Supreme Court decided on the applicability of the President's national security powers to seize private property. President Truman had ordered the Secretary of Commerce to take possession of and operate the mills in order to maintain steel production during the Korean War. The Supreme Court held that President Truman had neither constitutional nor statutory authority to seize the nation's strike-bound steel mills (the Court noted, however, that Congress would have had the constitutional authority to do so). Facts The setting of Youngstown took place during the Korean War. In 1951, a labor dispute had arisen between steel companies and their employees. As a result of the parties' failure to reach a collective bargaining agreement, the workers went on strike, which paused the production of much-needed steel for war materials. Fearing that such a stoppage would pose a threat to national security, President Harry S. Truman issued an executive order directing the Secretary of Commerce, Charles Sawyer, to seize the steel mills to keep them running. The steel companies brought action alleging that the seizure was unconstitutional. Procedural History The District Court held against Sawyer and issued a preliminary injunction preventing the Secretary from continuing the seizure and possession of the plants. Following the Court of Appeals stay on the District Court's injunction, the Supreme Court granted certiorari to decide the issue. Holding Ultimately, in a 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court held that President Truman's actions were unconstitutional, as they were not explicitly authorized by an act of Congress, nor could the action be reasonably construed as carrying out one of the authorities granted to the President. As to the government's argument that the order was authorized under the President's power as Commander in Chief, the Court responded that such powers did not include authorizing the President to seize private property to prevent labor disputes from interrupting production.

sections.Parties: The petitioners in No. 744 were Youngstown Sheet & Tube Company and other major steel producers, including Republic Steel, Bethlehem Steel, Jones & Laughlin, Armco and United States Steel, whose mills had been seized. The respondent was Charles Sawyer, Secretary of Commerce, who carried out the seizure; he was also the petitioner in the cross-case, No. 745. The United Steelworkers of America, CIO, whose threatened strike prompted the seizure, appeared as amicus supporting the Government. John W. Davis argued for the steel companies and Solicitor General Philip Perlman for the Secretary.
sections.Material Facts: In late 1951 a dispute arose between the steel companies and the United Steelworkers over terms of a new collective bargaining agreement. The union called a nationwide strike to begin on April 9, 1952. On April 8, 1952, believing a stoppage would jeopardize national defense, President Truman issued Executive Order 10340 directing the Secretary of Commerce to take possession of most of the steel mills and keep them running. The order cited no statute; it rested on the powers vested in the President by the Constitution and laws and as Commander in Chief. The Secretary seized the mills and directed their presidents to operate them as managers for the United States. The President reported to Congress on April 9 and again on April 21, but Congress took no action. In 1947 Congress had considered and rejected a proposal to authorize seizures in the Taft-Hartley Act, and two other statutes allowed seizures only under conditions not met here.
sections.Procedural History: The steel companies sued the Secretary in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia for a declaratory judgment and an injunction, arguing the seizure was unauthorized by statute or Constitution. On April 30, 1952, Judge Pine issued a preliminary injunction restraining the Secretary from continuing the seizure, 103 F. Supp. 569. The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit stayed the injunction the same day. Both sides petitioned for certiorari before judgment, which the Court granted on May 3. Argument was heard on May 12 and 13, 1952, and the Court decided the case on June 2, 1952, affirming the District Court by a vote of six to three. Justice Black wrote the opinion of the Court, and five Justices in the majority also wrote separately.
sections.Issue: Two questions were presented. First, was the case ripe for a decision on the constitutional validity of the Executive Order at the preliminary injunction stage, given the Government's argument that the companies could recover damages in the Court of Claims and so suffered no irreparable injury? Second, did the President have authority, either from an act of Congress or from his constitutional powers as Chief Executive and Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces, to order the Secretary of Commerce to seize and operate the nation's steel mills in order to prevent a strike that he believed would endanger national defense?
sections.Holding: The case was ripe: recovery in the Court of Claims was doubtful and the damages from seizure were hard to measure, so the District Court properly reached the merits. The Executive Order was not authorized by the Constitution or the laws and cannot stand. No statute expressly or impliedly authorized the seizure, and Congress in 1947 refused to grant seizure power. The order cannot be sustained as an exercise of the Commander in Chief's military power, which does not extend to taking possession of private property to settle labor disputes, nor under the general grant of executive power, because the order is lawmaking, a function the Constitution gives to Congress alone. The judgment of the District Court is affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Black wrote that the President's power, if any, to issue the order must stem either from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself. No statute authorized it, and when Congress wrote the Taft-Hartley Act in 1947 it considered and rejected seizure as a means of settling labor disputes, choosing instead mediation, a cooling-off period and injunctions; two other statutes allowed seizures only under conditions the Government did not claim to meet. The Commander in Chief Clause did not help. Even a broad view of that power over a theater of war could not extend to taking possession of private property to keep labor disputes from halting production; that is a job for the Nation's lawmakers. Nor could the seizure rest on the clauses vesting executive power in the President and directing him to take care that the laws be faithfully executed. The Constitution limits the President's lawmaking role to recommending laws and vetoing bad ones; it does not let him make laws. The order looked like a statute: it set out reasons, prescribed policy, and directed an official to implement it. The Founders entrusted the lawmaking power to Congress alone. The Court declined to give weight to the claim that other Presidents had seized businesses without congressional authority, holding that Congress had not thereby lost its exclusive power to make the laws necessary and proper to carry out all powers vested in the Government.

topics.lrs-o-executive-orders: An executive order is a form for exercising authority rather than its source: the steel seizure failed because neither the Constitution nor governing statutes authorized that action.
topics.lrs-s-article-i-vesting: Black's opinion rests on Article I vesting lawmaking in Congress and denies the President a lawmaking role; useful cross-reference for exam analysis of separation of powers.

learning.separateOpinions: Six to three, with five concurring opinions. Justice Frankfurter concurred, stressing that Congress had deliberately withheld seizure power in 1947 and that a systematic, unbroken executive practice known to Congress could gloss executive power, but none supported this seizure. Justice Douglas concurred, reasoning that seizure is a taking requiring compensation that only Congress can authorize. Justice Jackson concurred with his three-category framework: presidential power is at its maximum with congressional authorization, uncertain in a zone of twilight when Congress is silent, and at its lowest ebb when the President acts against the expressed or implied will of Congress, as here. Justice Burton concurred because Congress had prescribed procedures the President bypassed. Justice Clark concurred in the judgment, relying on the existence of statutory procedures. Chief Justice Vinson, joined by Justices Reed and Minton, dissented, invoking the emergency, the President's duty to preserve congressional programs, and historical precedents from Lincoln to Roosevelt.
